title: Read Secrets from C#
description: Use Azure.Security.KeyVault.Secrets to fetch secrets into ASP.NET Core without hardcoding credentials.

data.text: The `Azure.Security.KeyVault.Secrets` package lets you read, set, and delete secrets programmatically. In ASP.NET Core, you typically read secrets at startup and inject them as configuration.

data.title: Read a secret from Key Vault

data.text: ASP.NET Core configuration is a key-value pipeline. You can add a custom provider that reads from Key Vault, or use the built-in Azure Key Vault provider.

data.title: Add Key Vault to configuration
data.content: Register Key Vault as a configuration source in Program.cs.

data.title: Secret naming
data.text: Key Vault secret names can use `--` as section separators. The Azure Key Vault configuration provider maps `ConnectionStrings--Default` to `ConnectionStrings:Default`.
Key Vault calls are network operations. Cache secrets in memory or distributed cache to avoid throttling and reduce latency.

data.title: Simple in-memory secret cache
data.content: Cache secrets in a thread-safe dictionary with a TTL.

data.title: Read a database connection string from Key Vault
data.description: Move a hardcoded connection string into Key Vault and load it in ASP.NET Core.
steps: Add a secret named `ConnectionStrings--Default` to Key Vault
Add Key Vault to the configuration pipeline
Replace hardcoded `GetConnectionString` usage with the new pipeline
Run the app locally with `az login` and verify the connection string loads
data.expectedOutcome: The app starts, reads the connection string from Key Vault, and no secrets exist in appsettings.json.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use the Key Vault configuration provider for seamless integration with ASP.NET Core configuration
Cache secrets to reduce network calls and avoid throttling
Prefer `DefaultAzureCredential` so the same code works locally and in Azure
data.takeaway: Reading secrets from C# is straightforward once Key Vault is wired into the configuration pipeline.
